title: ACO Fundamentals: Attribution, Benchmarks & Shared Savings
summary: How ACOs work: patient attribution, spending benchmarks, shared savings and losses, and the Medicare Shared Savings Program structure.

objectives.text: Explain the three core mechanics of ACO payment: attribution, benchmark, shared savings
Describe the difference between one-sided and two-sided risk
Explain how MSSP tracks are structured and how they create a glide path to risk

children.text: Here is a question that sounds simple but is genuinely hard to answer: if a hospital successfully reduces its patients’ hospitalization rate by 15% through better care management, is that good news or bad news for the hospital’s finances? The instinctive answer is that it must be good news — fewer hospitalizations means healthier patients, which is surely the goal. But in a world where 40% of that hospital’s revenue still comes from fee-for-service Medicare and Medicaid payments, fewer hospitalizations means fewer inpatient admissions, which means fewer billed days, which means lower revenue. The hospital just cut its own income by doing its job better. This is not a hypothetical paradox — it is the central economic tension of the volume-to-value transition, experienced by virtually every health system that has seriously engaged with value-based care. Understanding this tension, and the financial mechanisms that VBC contract structures use to resolve it, is what this module is about.
The Financial Anatomy of a Shared Savings Contract

The Medicare Shared Savings Program is the most widely adopted VBC model in the United States, and shared savings is the financial mechanism at its core. Understanding how shared savings actually works — how the benchmark is set, how savings are calculated, and how they are distributed — is the foundation for understanding the economics of most VBC arrangements. The concept is straightforward: CMS calculates how much it would have expected to spend on your attributed patient population if they had remained in traditional fee-for-service Medicare, adjusted for their age, health status, and geographic cost factors. This projected spend is your “benchmark.” If your ACO’s actual spending on that population comes in below the benchmark, the difference is “savings.” You share those savings with CMS according to a pre-agreed formula — typically retaining 40–75% depending on your risk track and quality performance, with CMS keeping the remainder.

The devil, as always, is in the details. The benchmark calculation uses a three-year historical average of your patient population’s spending, adjusted upward by a national trend factor. For ACOs whose patient populations were already low-cost before joining the program, this creates an immediate structural problem: their benchmark is low, so even excellent care management produces modest absolute savings, making the shared savings payment insufficient to cover the care management infrastructure investment. This is called the “low benchmark problem,” and it is the primary reason that rural and safety-net ACOs, which often already operate lean systems with lower baseline utilization, struggle to generate shared savings large enough to justify Advanced APM participation costs. CMS has modified the benchmark methodology three times since 2012 in response to this problem, most recently in the Pathways to Success Rule of 2018 and the 2023 ACO Primary Care Flex Model, but the fundamental tension between historical benchmarking and equitable VBC participation for already-efficient providers remains unresolved.
Upside-Only vs. Two-Sided Risk: The Decision That Changes Everything

One of the most consequential decisions a provider organization makes when entering a shared savings arrangement is whether to accept only upside risk — where you share in savings if you beat the benchmark but owe nothing if you miss it — or two-sided risk, where you both share savings and repay losses if spending exceeds the benchmark. This choice has profound implications for the financial planning, working capital requirements, and organizational risk appetite of the participating entity. Upside-only arrangements (MSSP Track 1 and its successors) are appropriate for organizations beginning their VBC journey: they provide financial experience with population cost management without the catastrophic downside scenario of a major loss repayment obligation. Two-sided arrangements (the MSSP ENHANCED Track, and CMMI’s ACO REACH Model — the 2023 successor to Global and Professional Direct Contracting, which runs through December 31, 2026 and is to be succeeded by the Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model from January 1, 2027) offer higher shared savings percentages — sometimes up to 80% of savings — but require the organization to maintain actuarial reserves sufficient to cover a loss scenario, typically modeled at 1–3% of benchmark spending.

For a health system with $30 million in unrestricted net assets, maintaining a $2.5 million actuarial reserve for ACO REACH participation represents a 8.3% allocation of available capital to a risk management buffer — a rational investment if leadership has high confidence in the organization’s ability to manage population cost, but a significant commitment that requires board-level approval and careful opportunity cost analysis against other capital needs.
Bundled Payments: When a Single Price Covers an Entire Episode of Care

Bundled payment models take a different economic approach to aligning incentives than shared savings. Rather than holding a provider accountable for the total cost of care across an entire attributed population, bundled payments establish a single target price for all the care associated with a specific clinical episode — typically defined as a procedure or hospitalization plus 90 days of post-acute care. If the sum of all actual payments during the episode falls below the target price, the lead provider (typically the hospital or physician group that performed the primary procedure) retains the difference. If actual costs exceed the target, the lead provider repays the excess. The economic logic is straightforward: bundled payments create a direct financial incentive for the hospital performing a hip replacement to care about which skilled nursing facility the patient is discharged to, how long they stay there, and whether they end up readmitted — because all of those costs are included in the bundle.

BPCI Advanced, CMS’s voluntary bundled payment model, ran from October 1, 2018 through December 31, 2025, with 29 inpatient and 3 outpatient clinical episode categories at launch, ranging from major joint replacement and cardiac procedures to pneumonia and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease hospitalizations. Its final evaluation (The Lewin Group for CMS, August 2026) found that participants reduced Medicare episode payments in every model year — by $743 per episode on average in Model Years 1 and 2 and by about $1,000 per episode in Model Years 3 through 6 — and that the model produced about $800 million in net Medicare savings across its eight model years: net losses in Model Years 1–3, when reconciliation payments to participants exceeded the spending reductions, were outweighed by net savings once CMS redesigned target pricing in Model Year 4 (2021). Readmission rates were similar to the comparison group, although patients in Model Years 7–8 reported less favorable changes in functional status. Critically, the savings came primarily from post-acute care — fewer patients discharged to skilled nursing or inpatient rehabilitation facilities, skilled nursing stays about three days shorter, and skilled nursing payments about $500 lower per episode — rather than from reductions in the procedural care itself, confirming the bundled payment hypothesis that the primary driver of unnecessary cost in high-volume episodes is the post-acute care tail, not the procedure. CMS concluded that BPCI Advanced did not meet its criteria for expansion, and carried its lessons into the mandatory Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM), which began January 1, 2026.

The bundled payment evidence for joint replacement is about as clean as healthcare economics gets: when you make the hospital financially responsible for what happens after the patient leaves, patients spend less time in nursing homes, have fewer complications, and cost Medicare significantly less money. The same logic applies to any high-volume procedure with a predictable post-acute care pattern. The challenge is applying it to medical conditions where the post-acute trajectory is far less predictable.
Capitation: The Most Advanced — and Most Misunderstood — VBC Model

Capitation is the payment model that most completely aligns provider incentives with patient health outcomes, and the one that generates the most anxiety among providers who have not operated under it before. Under capitation, a provider or provider organization receives a fixed payment per enrolled member per month — the “PMPM” rate — and is responsible for delivering or arranging all covered healthcare services for that member, regardless of how much care they actually use. If the member uses more care than the PMPM covers, the provider absorbs the loss. If the member uses less, the provider retains the surplus. This structure creates the strongest possible financial incentive for prevention, care coordination, and early intervention — because every avoided hospitalization translates directly into retained revenue rather than lost fee-for-service income.

The anxiety around capitation is understandable but often misdirected. The concern most commonly expressed is that capitation incentivizes providers to withhold necessary care — to under-treat rather than over-treat. This concern is real and has historical basis: the managed care capitation models of the 1990s were frequently criticized for exactly this failure, and some HMO capitation arrangements did produce documented under-treatment in specific service categories. But the lesson of the 1990s HMO experience is not that capitation is inherently dangerous. It is that capitation without robust quality measurement, meaningful patient choice, and strong external accountability produces dangerous incentives. Modern capitation models — including Medicare Advantage plans and CMS’s ACO REACH program — include comprehensive quality metric frameworks with financial consequences for poor performance, minimum coverage requirements that prevent service restriction below evidence-based thresholds, and beneficiary rights to seek care outside the network when needed. The capitation model that exists in 2026 is substantively different from the managed care capitation of 1996.
How PMPM Rates Are Set: The Actuarial Core of Capitation

The financial success or failure of a capitation arrangement is largely determined before any patient is seen, at the point where the PMPM rate is negotiated or set. If the rate is set too low relative to the actual cost of providing care to the enrolled population, no amount of care management efficiency will produce a viable financial model. If the rate is set appropriately — reflecting the health acuity, demographic profile, and social complexity of the enrolled population — a well-managed capitated provider can generate margins of 3–8% while delivering care that is demonstrably better in quality and lower in total cost than the fee-for-service alternative. The actuarial process of setting a PMPM rate involves risk adjustment models that account for enrollee diagnoses, functional status, and social determinants of health, applied to utilization cost data from comparable populations. For Medicare Advantage plans, CMS sets the base rate using the county-level fee-for-service benchmark and adjusts it upward or downward based on each enrollee’s Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) risk score, a diagnosis-based model that attempts to predict expected healthcare utilization for that individual in the coming year.
The Volume-to-Value Transition: Why the Math Gets Hard Before It Gets Easy

The single most common financial mistake health systems make in VBC transitions is underestimating the revenue disruption of the transition period — the window, typically 18 to 36 months, during which care management investments have begun reducing utilization but VBC contract revenue has not yet scaled to replace the lost fee-for-service volume. Consider a regional health system generating $400 million in annual net patient revenue, with 30% of that revenue from inpatient admissions billed on a fee-for-service basis. The system joins MSSP and invests $2 million in care management infrastructure — care coordinators, a risk stratification platform, a post-discharge follow-up program — that begins generating measurable results in year one, reducing its attributed Medicare population’s hospitalization rate by 12%. That 12% reduction represents approximately 240 avoided admissions. At an average net revenue of $8,500 per admission, it also represents a $2.04 million reduction in fee-for-service inpatient revenue. The system’s MSSP shared savings payment for year one, based on total population savings, might be $1.4 million. Net financial impact of year one VBC investment: negative $640,000.

This math is not an argument against VBC. It is an argument for understanding VBC as a multi-year financial investment with a specific payback horizon, rather than a year-one revenue enhancement strategy. CMS’s own results show what is achievable at scale: in Performance Year 2024, Shared Savings Program ACOs generated gross savings of $651 per assigned beneficiary (shared between ACOs and Medicare) and net Medicare savings of $245, and 75% of the 476 participating ACOs earned performance payments. CMS publishes no standard figure for what ACOs spend on care management infrastructure, so the return on that investment has to be modeled from each organization’s own cost base. The problem is that most health system financial planning cycles operate on one-to-three year horizons, which are too short to capture the full economic benefit of VBC investment. Organizations that have successfully navigated the volume-to-value transition have done so by securing board approval for a five-to-seven year VBC investment thesis with explicit transition period loss projections, rather than attempting to justify each year’s VBC expenditure against that same year’s VBC revenue.

For CFOs and Finance Leaders: If your organization is evaluating ACO or Advanced APM participation, your financial model must explicitly project the transition period revenue displacement — the reduction in fee-for-service inpatient and ED revenue that will occur as care management succeeds. An ACO financial model that shows positive net revenue in year one almost certainly has a methodology error, either in the care management cost estimates or in the assumed savings rate. Realistic five-year models typically show a cumulative loss in years one and two, breakeven in year three, and meaningful positive return in years four and five. Present this model honestly to your board, or the VBC investment will be defunded the first time a quarterly loss appears.
Primary Care Investment as Economic Infrastructure

One of the most powerful and counterintuitive findings in health economics is that investment in primary care produces returns that are comparable to, and in many cases superior to, investment in specialty care infrastructure — not in terms of individual clinical case intensity, but in terms of total population health spending and outcomes. The economic mechanism is straightforward once articulated: primary care reduces the incidence of the expensive downstream events — hospitalizations, emergency visits, specialist procedures, complications of uncontrolled chronic disease — that account for the vast majority of total healthcare spending. A study published in Health Affairs in 2024 analyzing Medicare spending patterns across 306 hospital referral regions found that regions with above-median primary care physician supply had 11.2% lower total Medicare spending per beneficiary, 18.4% fewer preventable hospital admissions, and 14.7% lower 30-day readmission rates than regions with below-median primary care supply, after controlling for demographic and health status differences.

The economic return on primary care investment is particularly relevant for value-based care organizations making resource allocation decisions. Under fee-for-service, a hospital has limited financial incentive to invest in expanding primary care capacity in its community — more primary care visits may mean fewer specialist referrals and fewer hospitalizations, which means less hospital revenue. Under a capitated or shared savings VBC model, the same investment in primary care capacity is a direct cost reduction strategy: every diabetic patient who sees their primary care provider quarterly and maintains target HbA1c levels is a patient who is unlikely to generate an $18,000 diabetic complication admission. The VBC payment model converts primary care from a cost center competing with hospital services for capital allocation into a return-generating infrastructure investment — which is the single most important realignment that value-based payment architecture produces.

body.title: Care Management Interventions: What the Published Evaluations Found

children.text: The evidence in the table above carries an important lesson: the interventions that paid for themselves in trials were targeted ones — transition coaching for patients leaving the hospital, community health workers for patients with documented unmet social needs — while broad primary care payment models that spread enhanced payments across whole practice panels reduced hospital use without producing net Medicare savings. An organization implementing a care coordinator program without a functioning risk stratification system to identify which patients the coordinator should prioritize will see substantially lower returns — because care management applied uniformly across a population is far less efficient than care management targeted to the patients most likely to have high-cost events in the next 12 months. The technology readiness discussion in Module 4 is therefore directly connected to the economics of VBC investment: organizations that build population health data infrastructure before scaling care management programs generate significantly better returns than those that sequence these investments in reverse order.

Care coordination works when it is aimed at the right patients: its effectiveness depends on a functioning risk stratification system that identifies which patients are genuinely high-risk, not just high-cost in the prior year.

Post-discharge transition support has some of the strongest trial evidence in care management: in Coleman’s randomized trial of 750 older adults, transition coaching cut 30-day rehospitalizations from 11.9% to 8.3% and lowered six-month hospital costs, because the cost of coaching is small relative to the cost of a readmission.

Community health worker programs are the intervention most directly connected to social determinants of health — addressing food insecurity, housing instability, and transportation barriers that drive utilization patterns that clinical care alone cannot change — and Penn’s IMPaCT program returned $2.47 to Medicaid for every dollar invested, within a single fiscal year.

Advanced primary care transformation is the most comprehensive intervention, but the federal evidence is sobering: neither CPC+ nor Primary Care First produced net Medicare savings once their enhanced payments were counted, and CPC+ practices with incentives to control total cost of care, such as Shared Savings Program participants, did better at lowering costs — which is why primary care investment pays off most reliably inside a total-cost-of-care arrangement rather than as a stand-alone add-on.

The organizations that are winning in value-based care are not winning because they have better doctors or better patients. They are winning because they have better data, better targeting, and better financial discipline about which interventions they invest in and for which patient populations. VBC is fundamentally an information business with a clinical delivery layer on top.
Module 3 Summary: The Economics of VBC Reward Patience, Infrastructure, and Precision

The economics of value-based care are not complicated in their logic, but they are frequently misunderstood in their timing and their requirements. Shared savings arrangements reward population cost management, but only after a benchmark has been established and a minimum savings threshold has been crossed. Bundled payments reward episode cost efficiency, but require investment in post-acute care coordination infrastructure that most hospitals have historically not needed. Capitation rewards comprehensive population health management, but requires actuarial sophistication, quality measurement capability, and working capital reserves that are significant organizational commitments. All three model types have in common a multi-year investment horizon that is at odds with annual budget cycles, and a data infrastructure dependency that is at odds with the technology readiness of many rural and safety-net providers.

The economic case for making these investments nonetheless is visible in CMS’s own results: in Performance Year 2024, Shared Savings Program ACOs generated gross savings of $651 per assigned beneficiary and net Medicare savings of $245, with physician-led, low-revenue ACOs outperforming hospital-led ones ($319 versus $180 net per beneficiary) — returns that depend on care management infrastructure maturing and on the organization’s ability to identify and target high-risk patients. The organizations that have reached this performance level did not arrive there by treating VBC as a compliance exercise or a contract opportunity. They treated it as a fundamental redesign of how they organize and deliver care, supported by a financial model that explicitly anticipated and planned for the transition period losses that are the unavoidable cost of that redesign. Module 4 examines the technology infrastructure that makes this financial performance possible.

Review your organization’s current VBC contract portfolio and categorize each contract by model type: shared savings (upside only or two-sided), bundled payment, or capitation. For each contract, identify whether you have a financial model projecting per-beneficiary investment cost, expected savings rate, and net financial benefit over a five-year horizon.

Ask your CFO to quantify the annual fee-for-service revenue at risk from your care management programs — the inpatient admissions and emergency visits that your VBC interventions are intended to prevent, translated into net revenue impact. Compare this to your projected shared savings or capitation savings. If the net is negative, verify your model is using a five-year, not a one-year, planning horizon.

Review the evidence in the care management intervention table in this module and identify which intervention types your organization is currently investing in. For each intervention, assess whether you have a functioning risk stratification system that targets the intervention to high-risk patients rather than applying it uniformly across your attributed population.

Assess your organization’s actuarial reserve capacity for two-sided risk participation. If your unrestricted net assets are below $15 million, upside-only MSSP participation is the appropriate starting point. If your unrestricted net assets exceed $30 million and you have three or more years of MSSP experience, a formal analysis of ENHANCED track participation, or of CMMI’s LEAD Model (the ACO REACH successor beginning January 1, 2027), is warranted.

Module 3 Key Takeaway: The economics of value-based care favor organizations that plan in five-year cycles, invest in care management infrastructure before scaling VBC contract volume, and understand the specific financial mechanics of their contract type at the level of the benchmark calculation and the savings distribution formula. VBC is not a revenue strategy for the next fiscal year. It is a business model for the next decade — one that rewards the organizations that build the infrastructure, accept the transition period losses, and stay the course long enough for the compounding returns of mature care management to materialize.

The center panel shows the ROI comparison across six care management intervention types as a horizontal bar chart, sorted by ROI ratio, with investment cost and savings bars color-coded in contrasting colors. The right panel shows a scatter plot of 200 MSSP ACOs with years of participation on the x-axis and net savings per beneficiary on the y-axis, illustrating the maturity curve with a regression line showing the inflection point at year three to four of participation. Data source: CMS MSSP Financial and Quality Results 2024.

It is an argument for understanding VBC as a multi-year financial investment with a specific payback horizon, rather than a year-one revenue enhancement strategy. CMS’s own results show what is achievable at scale: in Performance Year 2024, Shared Savings Program ACOs generated gross savings of $651 per assigned beneficiary (shared between ACOs and Medicare) and net Medicare savings of $245, and 75% of the 476 participating ACOs earned performance payments. CMS publishes no standard figure for what ACOs spend on care management infrastructure, so the return on that investment has to be modeled from each organization’s own cost base. The problem is that most health system financial planning cycles operate on one-to-three year horizons, which are too short to capture the full economic benefit of VBC investment. Organizations that have successfully navigated the volume-to-value transition have done so by securing board approval for a five-to-seven year VBC investment thesis with explicit transition period loss projections, rather than attempting to justify each year’s VBC expenditure against that same year’s VBC revenue.
content_blocks.heading: The Volume-to-Value Transition: Why the Math Gets Hard Before It Gets Easy

content_blocks.body: For CFOs and Finance Leaders: If your organization is evaluating ACO or Advanced APM participation, your financial model must explicitly project the transition period revenue displacement — the reduction in fee-for-service inpatient and ED revenue that will occur as care management succeeds. An ACO financial model that shows positive net revenue in year one almost certainly has a methodology error, either in the care management cost estimates or in the assumed savings rate. Realistic five-year models typically show a cumulative loss in years one and two, breakeven in year three, and meaningful positive return in years four and five. Present this model honestly to your board, or the VBC investment will be defunded the first time a quarterly loss appears.
content_blocks.heading: Key Concept

content_blocks.body:
One of the most powerful and counterintuitive findings in health economics is that investment in primary care produces returns that are comparable to, and in many cases superior to, investment in specialty care infrastructure — not in terms of individual clinical case intensity, but in terms of total population health spending and outcomes. The economic mechanism is straightforward once articulated: primary care reduces the incidence of the expensive downstream events — hospitalizations, emergency visits, specialist procedures, complications of uncontrolled chronic disease — that account for the vast majority of total healthcare spending. A study published in Health Affairs in 2024 analyzing Medicare spending patterns across 306 hospital referral regions found that regions with above-median primary care physician supply had 11.2% lower total Medicare spending per beneficiary, 18.4% fewer preventable hospital admissions, and 14.7% lower 30-day readmission rates than regions with below-median primary care supply, after controlling for demographic and health status differences.

The economic return on primary care investment is particularly relevant for value-based care organizations making resource allocation decisions. Under fee-for-service, a hospital has limited financial incentive to invest in expanding primary care capacity in its community — more primary care visits may mean fewer specialist referrals and fewer hospitalizations, which means less hospital revenue. Under a capitated or shared savings VBC model, the same investment in primary care capacity is a direct cost reduction strategy: every diabetic patient who sees their primary care provider quarterly and maintains target HbA1c levels is a patient who is unlikely to generate an $18,000 diabetic complication admission. The VBC payment model converts primary care from a cost center competing with hospital services for capital allocation into a return-generating infrastructure investment — which is the single most important realignment that value-based payment architecture produces.

The evidence in the table above carries an important lesson: the interventions that paid for themselves in trials were targeted ones — transition coaching for patients leaving the hospital, community health workers for patients with documented unmet social needs — while broad primary care payment models that spread enhanced payments across whole practice panels reduced hospital use without producing net Medicare savings. An organization implementing a care coordinator program without a functioning risk stratification system to identify which patients the coordinator should prioritize will see substantially lower returns — because care management applied uniformly across a population is far less efficient than care management targeted to the patients most likely to have high-cost events in the next 12 months. The technology readiness discussion in Module 4 is therefore directly connected to the economics of VBC investment: organizations that build population health data infrastructure before scaling care management programs generate significantly better returns than those that sequence these investments in reverse order.

Care coordination works when it is aimed at the right patients: its effectiveness depends on a functioning risk stratification system that identifies which patients are genuinely high-risk, not just high-cost in the prior year.

Post-discharge transition support has some of the strongest trial evidence in care management: in Coleman’s randomized trial of 750 older adults, transition coaching cut 30-day rehospitalizations from 11.9% to 8.3% and lowered six-month hospital costs, because the cost of coaching is small relative to the cost of a readmission.

Community health worker programs are the intervention most directly connected to social determinants of health — addressing food insecurity, housing instability, and transportation barriers that drive utilization patterns that clinical care alone cannot change — and Penn’s IMPaCT program returned $2.47 to Medicaid for every dollar invested, within a single fiscal year.

Advanced primary care transformation is the most comprehensive intervention, but the federal evidence is sobering: neither CPC+ nor Primary Care First produced net Medicare savings once their enhanced payments were counted, and CPC+ practices with incentives to control total cost of care, such as Shared Savings Program participants, did better at lowering costs — which is why primary care investment pays off most reliably inside a total-cost-of-care arrangement rather than as a stand-alone add-on.
content_blocks.heading: Primary Care Investment as Economic Infrastructure

content_blocks.body: The organizations that are winning in value-based care are not winning because they have better doctors or better patients. They are winning because they have better data, better targeting, and better financial discipline about which interventions they invest in and for which patient populations. VBC is fundamentally an information business with a clinical delivery layer on top.
content_blocks.heading: Quote

content_blocks.body:
The economics of value-based care are not complicated in their logic, but they are frequently misunderstood in their timing and their requirements. Shared savings arrangements reward population cost management, but only after a benchmark has been established and a minimum savings threshold has been crossed. Bundled payments reward episode cost efficiency, but require investment in post-acute care coordination infrastructure that most hospitals have historically not needed. Capitation rewards comprehensive population health management, but requires actuarial sophistication, quality measurement capability, and working capital reserves that are significant organizational commitments. All three model types have in common a multi-year investment horizon that is at odds with annual budget cycles, and a data infrastructure dependency that is at odds with the technology readiness of many rural and safety-net providers.

The economic case for making these investments nonetheless is visible in CMS’s own results: in Performance Year 2024, Shared Savings Program ACOs generated gross savings of $651 per assigned beneficiary and net Medicare savings of $245, with physician-led, low-revenue ACOs outperforming hospital-led ones ($319 versus $180 net per beneficiary) — returns that depend on care management infrastructure maturing and on the organization’s ability to identify and target high-risk patients. The organizations that have reached this performance level did not arrive there by treating VBC as a compliance exercise or a contract opportunity. They treated it as a fundamental redesign of how they organize and deliver care, supported by a financial model that explicitly anticipated and planned for the transition period losses that are the unavoidable cost of that redesign. Module 4 examines the technology infrastructure that makes this financial performance possible.

Review your organization’s current VBC contract portfolio and categorize each contract by model type: shared savings (upside only or two-sided), bundled payment, or capitation. For each contract, identify whether you have a financial model projecting per-beneficiary investment cost, expected savings rate, and net financial benefit over a five-year horizon.

Ask your CFO to quantify the annual fee-for-service revenue at risk from your care management programs — the inpatient admissions and emergency visits that your VBC interventions are intended to prevent, translated into net revenue impact. Compare this to your projected shared savings or capitation savings. If the net is negative, verify your model is using a five-year, not a one-year, planning horizon.

Review the evidence in the care management intervention table in this module and identify which intervention types your organization is currently investing in. For each intervention, assess whether you have a functioning risk stratification system that targets the intervention to high-risk patients rather than applying it uniformly across your attributed population.

Assess your organization’s actuarial reserve capacity for two-sided risk participation. If your unrestricted net assets are below $15 million, upside-only MSSP participation is the appropriate starting point. If your unrestricted net assets exceed $30 million and you have three or more years of MSSP experience, a formal analysis of ENHANCED track participation, or of CMMI’s LEAD Model (the ACO REACH successor beginning January 1, 2027), is warranted.
content_blocks.heading: Module 3 Summary: The Economics of VBC Reward Patience, Infrastructure, and Precision

content_blocks.body: Module 3 Key Takeaway: The economics of value-based care favor organizations that plan in five-year cycles, invest in care management infrastructure before scaling VBC contract volume, and understand the specific financial mechanics of their contract type at the level of the benchmark calculation and the savings distribution formula. VBC is not a revenue strategy for the next fiscal year. It is a business model for the next decade — one that rewards the organizations that build the infrastructure, accept the transition period losses, and stay the course long enough for the compounding returns of mature care management to materialize.
